content.title: About
content.content: Toasted bread that blends traditional recipes from Italy, Greece and Armenia, offering a crisp crust and a soft, aromatic crumb. The dough is usually made from wheat flour, olive oil, yogurt or kefir, and often flavored with herbs such as oregano, rosemary or cumin, giving it a distinct Mediterranean taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Italian focaccia, Greek pita and Armenian lavash each have unique shapes and thicknesses.
Traditional Armenian bread is baked in a tandoor, imparting a smoky flavor.
Toasting enhances aroma and creates a crunchier crust while reducing moisture, extending shelf life.
In the Mediterranean, bread is commonly served with olive oil, feta cheese or hummus.
Ancient Greek myth says bread was a gift from the gods and used in rituals.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Bread provides a steady release of energy thanks to slowly digestible carbohydrates.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions contain dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, niacin and folate help metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Bread supplies iron, magnesium and phosphorus, important for blood and bone health.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: When kefir or yogurt is used in the dough, it can promote beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which can cause issues for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White toasted bread can raise blood sugar quickly, which is undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Salt and fat
items.content: Some recipes use generous amounts of salt or olive oil, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Certain versions may include seeds (sesame, poppy) that trigger allergies.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toasted bread works well as a base for sandwiches, topped with olive oil, avocado, cheese, ham or vegetables. It can be crumbled into casseroles or served alongside soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bread in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, place it in an airtight container in the refrigerator (up to a week) or freeze (up to 3 months). Warm in the oven before serving to restore a crunchy crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Duck is a waterfowl raised for its meat. Roasted duck with crispy skin is a delicacy in many world cuisines. The skin is rich in fat, which when properly cooked becomes aromatic and crunchy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ducks are capable of migration, but most commercial birds are kept on closed farms.
Duck skin is high in collagen, which forms a golden crust during prolonged roasting.
In China, Peking duck is a classic dish where the skin is the star of the flavor.
Duck fat is prized for frying and in cosmetics because of its softening properties.
Duck meat contains more iron than chicken.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Duck meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: The iron in duck meat is readily absorbed and helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Duck supplies B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Polyunsaturated fats
items.content: Duck fat contains omega‑6 and modest amounts of omega‑3 fatty acids, beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Collagen in the skin
items.content: When roasted, the skin releases collagen, which may aid skin elasticity and joint health.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Duck skin is very fatty; overconsumption can lead to excess calories and elevated cholesterol.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked duck may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 165 °F (74 °C).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird meat.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Duck is high in purines, which can be problematic for people with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Duck can be roasted whole, cut into portions, or used cold in salads. The skin is eaten crispy, seasoned with salt, spices, or a glaze. Serve with fruit sauces, vegetable sides, or traditional Chinese pancakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked roasted duck in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 165 °F (74 °C) before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: The fruit flavored drink in powder form is intended to be reconstituted with water. It contains dried fruit extracts, sugar or sugar substitutes, flavorings, and sometimes added vitamins. When dissolved, it yields a refreshing, sweet‑tasting beverage.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Powdered drinks are convenient for transport and long‑term storage because they do not require refrigeration.
A wide range of flavors is available: orange, lemon, strawberry, mango, and more.
The powder is often fortified with vitamin C and other micronutrients.
In many countries these drinks are popular in school cafeterias as a quick source of energy.
Sugar content varies from fully sweetened to low‑calorie versions using sweeteners.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A reconstituted drink helps replenish body fluids, especially in hot weather or after exercise.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Sugar or sweeteners provide rapid glucose, which can raise energy levels.

items.title: Ease of consumption
items.content: The powder is easy to dose and prepare, making it convenient for travel and outdoor activities.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Powdered drinks typically contain no fat, fitting well into low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: High sugar levels can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some variants may contain flavorings or colorants that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Excess vitamin C
items.content: Very large doses of vitamin C may cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Improper dilution
items.content: Using too little water results in an overly concentrated drink that may irritate the stomach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix one serving of powder (usually 1–2 sachets) with 200–250 ml of cold water, stirring until fully dissolved. Ice, fresh fruit slices, or mint can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry powder in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the package tightly closed to prevent moisture absorption.

soft-drink-cola-fruit-or-vanilla-flavore.title: Soft drink, cola, fruit or vanilla flavored

content.title: About
content.content: A soft drink with cola, fruit or vanilla flavor is a non‑alcoholic beverage made by carbonating water and adding sugar (or sweeteners), flavorings, acid (usually phosphoric), and sometimes caffeine. The cola version has a characteristic caramel taste, the fruit version offers bright berry or tropical notes, and the vanilla version provides a smooth sweet vanilla nuance.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial carbonated drink was sold in England in 1767.
Cola drinks are named after the kola nut, originally used as a caffeine source.
Fruit sodas often use fruit concentrates, but most flavors are synthetically produced.
Vanilla‑flavored soda appeared in the 1970s as an alternative to traditional cola.
Carbonation enhances the perception of freshness and sweetness.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The water base helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Quick Energy
items.content: Sugar (or its substitutes) provides a rapid rise in blood glucose, giving a short‑term energy boost.

items.title: Stimulation
items.content: Caffeine, present in many versions, can improve alertness and reduce fatigue.

items.title: Vitamin Content
items.content: Some fruit‑flavored variants are fortified with vitamin C and other antioxidants.

items.title: Flavor Enhancement
items.content: Carbonation stimulates taste buds, making the drink taste brighter.

items.title: High Sugar Content
items.content: Regular consumption can contribute to weight gain, tooth decay, and increased risk of metabolic diseases.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Phosphoric and citric acids may irritate the stomach lining and erode tooth enamel.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Excess intake can cause insomnia, anxiety, and rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Artificial Sweeteners
items.content: They may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in some individuals.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Certain flavorings can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Consume
content.content: Soft drinks are typically served chilled in a glass or bottle. They can be used in cocktails, mixed drinks, and culinary applications such as marinades, glazes, and desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days to retain carbonation.

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed potatoes are a dish made from diced potatoes slowly cooked in broth or sauce together with vegetables, spices, and sometimes meat. The potatoes keep their shape while absorbing a tender, flavorful taste from the long simmering.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stewing retains more vitamins and minerals compared with boiling.
In traditional Russian cuisine, stewed potatoes are often cooked with carrots, onions, and bay leaf.
Some regions add tomato paste or cream for a richer flavor.
Stewed potatoes are frequently used as a base for casseroles and ragouts.
When stored properly in the refrigerator, the dish can last 3‑4 days.

items.title: Rich source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Stewing preserves part of the vitamin C, important for immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The fiber in potatoes aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Stewed potatoes deliver slow‑releasing energy, helpful for maintaining stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Beta‑carotene (in colored varieties)
items.content: Orange and yellow potatoes contain provitamin A, supporting vision and skin health.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Excessive salt addition can increase hypertension risk; control the amount of salt used.

items.title: Glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Solanine presence
items.content: Green spots and sprouts contain solanine—a toxin that should be removed before cooking.

items.title: Nightshade allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to potatoes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Stewed potatoes can be served as a main dish, a side to meat or fish, incorporated into salads, casseroles, and soups. Reheat in the microwave or skillet, adding fresh herbs for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months; thaw and reheat before serving.

tea-iced-instant-black-unsweetened-dry.title: Tea, iced, instant, black, unsweetened, dry

content.title: About
content.content: Instant unsweetened black tea is a dry powder made from black tea leaves that dissolves quickly in hot or cold water. It is perfect for preparing iced tea at home and contains no added sugar, offering a clean, slightly astringent flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black tea is the most consumed tea worldwide after green tea.
Instant tea was invented in the early 20th century for soldiers and travelers.
Dry instant tea has a longer shelf life than leaf tea due to low moisture content.
Black tea is rich in polyphenols that give it its characteristic aroma and color.
Unsweetened versions are often used as a base for fruit and herbal blends.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Black tea contains polyphenols that help neutralize free radicals and protect cells.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Moderate regular consumption may improve vascular function and lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Enhanced focus
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, increasing alertness and concentration.

items.title: Hydration without extra calories
items.content: Unsweetened instant tea is a low‑calorie beverage that helps maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Tannins can support digestion and reduce the feeling of heaviness after meals.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat with excessive intake.

items.title: Iron absorption
items.content: Tannins may reduce non‑heme iron absorption, so people with anemia should drink tea between meals.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: Rarely, an allergic reaction to tea components can occur.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: For hot tea, dissolve 1‑2 g (about 1 teaspoon) of dry powder in 200 ml of boiling water and stir until fully dissolved. For iced tea, dissolve the powder in a small amount of hot water, then add cold water or ice, optionally garnish with lemon slices or mint.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the package of dry instant tea in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Properly stored, it remains good for up to 2 years.
